<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md -->

# Messaging

No encrypted messaging protocol is inherently superior. Each one trades metadata exposure, forward secrecy and reach against the others, and the right trade depends on who the user is writing to. kernl therefore supports several and ranks none ([D-009](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-009)). A provider describes its own properties truthfully; the shell shows the description and lets the user choose.

## The provider contract

A `MessagingProvider` in `@kernl/messaging` is a pluggable module with one contract:

```ts
interface MessagingProvider {
  readonly id: string;              // conversation-id prefix: 'private', 'legacy', 'ratchet'
  readonly name: string;            // user-facing, no protocol vocabulary
  readonly description: string;     // one sentence for the picker
  readonly properties: SecurityProperties;
  availability(): ProviderAvailability;
  createBackend(): MessagingBackend;
}
```

`createBackend()` returns a `MessagingBackend`: `status`, `conversations`, `messages`, `send`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe` and an optional `close`. The shape is structurally identical to kehto's `DmAdapter`, so a backend can be handed to `createDmService` without translation while this package stays free of a kehto dependency. The wire types (`DmConversation`, `DmMessage`, `DmSendRequest` and friends) come from `@napplet/core`. Every method except `send` may return a value or a promise.

The package holds no relay code, signer or store. A provider is built with `defineProvider(definition, deps)`, where `definition` is the fixed, user-facing part (`id`, `name`, `description`, `properties`) and `deps` is what the shell injects:

```ts
interface ProviderDeps {
  createBackend: () => MessagingBackend;     // called once per enable; the registry owns the instance
  available: () => ProviderAvailability;     // { available: true } or { available: false, reason }
}
```

The three built-in factories (`createPrivateMessagesProvider`, `createLegacyMessagesProvider`, `createRatchetMessagesProvider`) take the same `ProviderDeps` and supply the definition themselves. In the shell, `@kernl/core`'s `createDefaultMessaging` builds each provider's `ProviderDeps` from `KernlOptions.messagingBackends` and nothing else: `createBackend` calls the factory the host supplied, and a provider without one reports itself unavailable. `apps/web` supplies none today, so all three are unavailable in the live shell ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#messaging-providers-in-the-live-shell)). In tests and the preview, `createBackend` returns `createMemoryBackend()`. See `providers.feature`, scenario "availability and the backend come from the shell".

## Security properties

`SecurityProperties` is a fixed set of fields. Every field except `specification` is required, and the shell renders them verbatim with no summary score:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `forwardSecrecy` | Compromise of today's keys does not reveal yesterday's messages. |
| `postCompromiseSecurity` | The session heals after a compromise once both parties exchange messages. |
| `metadataProtection` | `none`, `partial` or `strong`: how much a network observer learns about who talks to whom and when. |
| `requiresSameClient` | The correspondent must use a client that speaks this provider. |
| `groups` | Conversations with more than two participants are supported. |
| `specification` | Optional. Where the protocol is specified. Shown in these docs, not in the public UI. |
| `experimental` | The provider is still changing and may lose history between versions. |

`describeProvider(provider)` turns them into the six rows the picker shows, in this order and with these labels: `Forward secrecy`, `Recovers after a key compromise`, `Metadata protection`, `Correspondent needs the same app`, `Group conversations`, `Experimental`. Booleans render as `yes`/`no`; `metadataProtection` renders as is; `specification` is left out so no protocol name reaches the UI ([D-006](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-006)).

## The three providers

| Provider id | Name | `specification` | What the specification is | Forward secrecy | Post-compromise security | Metadata protection | Same client required | Groups | Experimental |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `private` | Private messages | `'NIP-17'` | Gift-wrapped private messages: kind 14 rumours sealed in kind 13, wrapped in kind 1059 with a random key | no | no | `partial`: the wrap hides sender and timing from relays, the recipient's inbox relays still see delivery | no | yes | no |
| `legacy` | Legacy messages | `'NIP-04'` | Direct messages: kind 4, shared-secret encryption | no | no | `none`: sender, recipient and timing are public on the event | no | no | no |
| `ratchet` | Ratchet sessions | `'nostr-double-ratchet (draft)'` | A double-ratchet session protocol over nostr, still a draft | yes | yes | `partial`: per-message ephemeral keys hide the long-term identities, relays still see timing | yes | no | yes |

The descriptions the picker shows: `private` "Sealed messages that hide who is talking to whom from the network."; `legacy` "The original direct-message format. Readable by the widest range of apps, but who you talk to is visible on the network."; `ratchet` "Per-session keys that change with every message. Both sides need an app that supports it."

Three things the table says that the picker says too:

- `legacy` is marked as metadata-exposing because it is. It exists because many correspondents can read nothing else, and the user is told that before choosing it.
- `private` has no forward secrecy. A gift wrap protects metadata, not past messages, and the picker does not claim otherwise.
- `ratchet` is available only when the shell's `available()` says so. The package does not decide the reason; kernl's `createDefaultMessaging` supplies `no-runtime` (`MESSAGING_UNAVAILABLE_REASONS.ratchet`), `enable()` rethrows it as `unavailable:no-runtime`, and `list()` reports it so the picker can show the provider greyed with that reason. Its specification is a draft and the provider is flagged `experimental`.

## The registry

The shell holds exactly one `MessagingRegistry`, built with `createMessagingRegistry({ preferences?, onChange? })`. It owns the backend instances:

- `register(provider)` adds a provider. Nothing is enabled by registration unless the saved `preferences.enabled` list names the provider; then it is enabled at once if available, and left disabled (reporting why through `list()`) if not. A second registration of the same id throws `invalid:duplicate-provider`.
- `enable(id)` calls `availability()` and throws `unavailable:<reason>` when the provider cannot run; otherwise it calls `createBackend()` once and keeps the instance. Enabling an enabled provider does nothing. Unknown ids throw `invalid:unknown-provider`.
- `disable(id)` calls the backend's `close?()` and drops it. If the default pointed at it, the default is cleared.
- `setDefault(id)` names the provider for sends that name no provider and no conversation. The provider must be enabled, else `invalid:provider-not-enabled`. A saved `defaultProvider` is restored when that provider registers, unless `setDefault` was called first.
- `preferences()` returns a frozen `{ enabled, defaultProvider? }` snapshot; `onChange` receives the same snapshot after every change.
- `composite()` returns one `MessagingBackend` spanning every enabled provider, for the NAP `dm` service. It is the same instance on every call and sees providers come and go.
- `close()` closes every backend and leaves the preferences untouched, so a shutdown never erases what the user chose. A closed registry is not reused.

See `registry.feature`, scenarios "saved preferences enable providers as they register" and "closing the registry closes every backend and keeps the preferences".

## The composite backend

The NAP `dm` domain is a projection over every enabled provider. `createCompositeBackend(resolveEnabled, getDefault)` builds it, and the only thing an applet can observe is the id namespace:

- Every conversation and message id leaving the composite is `"<providerId>:<innerId>"`, built by `namespaceId`. `private:direct:ab,cd` is the conversation `direct:ab,cd` as the `private` provider knows it. The inner id may itself contain `:`; `splitId` splits on the first one only.
- Ids arriving from the applet are split to find the provider. An id without a prefix, or with a prefix no enabled provider owns, rejects with `invalid:unknown-provider`.
- `conversations()` with a cursor routes to the provider named in the cursor and passes the inner cursor through. Without a cursor and with exactly one provider enabled, the provider's page is returned with its cursor namespaced (`private:2`). With several providers, every provider's page is fetched, the conversations are merged and sorted by `updatedAt` descending (conversations without activity sort last), `limit` is applied to the merged list, and the page carries no cursor, because no single provider can resume a merged page.
- `messages()` routes by the conversation prefix and prefixes the ids on the way out.
- `send()` routes by the conversation id when there is one, else by the `provider` field (`WithProvider<DmSendRequest>`) the shell adds when the user picks a provider for a new conversation, else by the default provider. An unknown provider rejects with `invalid:unknown-provider`; no default, or a default that is no longer enabled, rejects with `unavailable:no-default-provider`.
- `subscribe()` with a conversation id subscribes on that provider; without one it subscribes on every enabled provider and fans the messages in, prefixed. Subscription ids are `composite-<n>`. Unsubscribing skips providers disabled in the meantime, since disabling already closed their backend, and reports `ok: false` if any surviving provider did.
- `status()` merges: `available` if any provider is, the first `ownerPubkey` found, the union of `implementations` and `capabilities`.
- `close()` on the composite is a no-op. The registry owns backend lifetimes.

An applet that uses `dm` therefore sees one inbox. Which provider carries a given conversation is visible in its id, and the shell shows it as a label the user can change for new conversations. See `composite.feature`.

## The in-memory backend

`createMemoryBackend({ owner?, available?, now? })` is a complete `MessagingBackend` with no network, used by the shell's offline preview and by every feature in this package. Conversations are keyed `direct:<pubkey>` or `group:<pubkey>,<pubkey>` over the sorted correspondents with the owner removed; `send()` stores the message as `sent` (id `msg-<n>`, or the request's `clientMessageId`) and notifies subscribers; `deliver({ senderPubkey, content, conversationId?, createdAt? })` plays the other side and stores a `received` message; unread counts are the number of `received` messages; cursors are numeric offsets with default page sizes of 50 conversations and 100 messages. `send()` rejects with `invalid:no-recipients`, `invalid:unknown-conversation` or `unavailable:offline`; reads keep working offline so a preview can still show history. See `memory-backend.feature`.

## Error reasons

| Reason | Thrown by |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid:duplicate-provider` | `register` |
| `invalid:unknown-provider` | `enable`, `disable` (unknown id); composite routing of ids, cursors and `provider` hints |
| `unavailable:<reason>` | `enable` when `availability()` is false; `<reason>` is the shell's word |
| `invalid:provider-not-enabled` | `setDefault` |
| `unavailable:no-default-provider` | composite `send` with no conversation, no hint and no usable default |
| `invalid:no-recipients`, `invalid:unknown-conversation`, `unavailable:offline` | memory backend `send` |

## Related

- [Add a messaging provider](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/add-a-messaging-provider.md)
- [`@kernl/messaging`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/messaging.md)

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md -->

# Decisions

The architecture decisions behind kernl, one entry per `D-NNN`. Every `D-NNN` mentioned in these docs links to its entry here, at the anchor `#d-nnn`. The log is `DECISIONS.md` at the root of the source repository, which is private during the alpha; this page includes that file verbatim when the docs are built, so it is never a second copy that can drift.

Architecture decisions for kernl, newest last. Each entry records what was decided, why, and what it would take to reverse it. A decision stays here after it is reversed; it gets a `Superseded by` line instead of being deleted.

Format: `D-NNN · title` → Context, Decision, Consequences, Reversal cost.

---

## D-001 · kernl composes kehto; it does not fork it

**Context.** kehto publishes `@kehto/{acl,firewall,runtime,shell,services,nip,wm}` as the unopinionated NIP-5D toolkit. kernl is the opinionated shell. Two of kehto's seams are narrower than kernl wants: `ShellAdapter` does not forward `getFocusContext`, `onFirewallEvent` or `firewallPersistence` to the runtime, and `createRuntime` hardcodes the ACL default policy to `'permissive'`. The transport internals (`createNip5dTransport`, `createShellReadyState`) are not exported, so kernl cannot assemble its own bridge from kehto parts.

**Decision.** kernl depends on the published `@kehto/*` packages at pinned minor ranges and uses `createShellBridge` unchanged. Behaviour kehto does not expose is built in front of the bridge, not inside a fork:

- Focus-aware rate limiting runs in `@kernl/guard` using the pure `@kehto/firewall` `evaluate()` engine with focus supplied by kernl's window manager. The runtime's built-in firewall is additionally tightened through `bridge.runtime.firewallState`.
- A restrictive grant posture is produced with `capabilities.resolveEnvironment`, which narrows the advertised domains per applet identity until the user grants them, plus explicit `aclState.grant` calls. The runtime's permissive default is never reached for a domain the user has not granted.

**Consequences.** Four upstream gaps are recorded against kehto/web rather than patched locally: (1) forward the firewall hooks through `ShellAdapter`; (2) let the host choose the ACL default policy; (3) offer a pre-dispatch hook on port traffic, since `onNappletMessage` is observe-only; (4) expose a setter for the runtime firewall's `unfocusedMultiplier`. When any of them lands, the corresponding kernl layer shrinks (see D-012).

**Reversal cost.** Low. Both local layers sit behind interfaces in `@kernl/guard` and `@kernl/core` and can be deleted when upstream provides the hook.

## D-002 · applesauce v7 is the only event layer

**Context.** kehto's reference runtime (Paja) uses `nostr-tools` `SimplePool`. kernl's first opinion is that applesauce is the event layer.

**Decision.** `applesauce-core` (`EventStore`), `applesauce-relay` (`RelayPool`), `applesauce-signers`, `applesauce-accounts` (`AccountManager`), `applesauce-loaders` and `applesauce-factory` are the only libraries kernl source imports for events, relays, signing and accounts. `nostr-tools` stays a transitive peer dependency required by kehto and applesauce; kernl source does not import it. kehto's `RelayPoolLike`, `RelayPoolServiceOptions` and `DmRelayPool` contracts are satisfied by thin adapters over one shared `RelayPool` in `@kernl/core/applesauce`.

**Consequences.** One pool, one store, one account manager per shell. A guard test fails the build if `nostr-tools` is imported from kernl source.

**Reversal cost.** High by design. The adapters are small, but the opinion is the point.

## D-003 · Every kehto mitigation ships on, in its strict profile

**Context.** Opinion three in `SOUL.md`.

**Decision.** `@kernl/guard` exposes three profiles, `strict`, `balanced` and `relaxed`. The shell boots in `strict`. The profile can be loosened per applet by the user through the grants panel, never globally by configuration. The mitigations and their defaults are listed in `docs/concepts/guard.md` and surfaced in the UI as a readable list with reasons.

**Consequences.** Some applets will hit limits in `strict`. The guard emits an event for every rejection and deferral so the user can see what happened and decide.

**Status in the first draft.** The profile is shell-wide and not persisted: `GuardFacade.setProfile` rebuilds the single pipeline, and windows already open keep the runtime rates installed at mount. Per-applet, remembered loosening is the target this decision describes and is tracked in `docs/roadmap.md`. The default remains `strict` on every boot, so the gap errs toward the user.

**Reversal cost.** A one-line profile change for a user; a `SOUL.md` amendment for the project.

## D-004 · Four packages, one app, one docs site

**Context.** The repository needs a shape that lets docs, tests and publishing stay per-package without forcing the shell UI into a framework-free constraint.

**Decision.**

| Workspace | Name | Role | Framework |
|---|---|---|---|
| `packages/guard` | `@kernl/guard` | Ingress flood control, visibility gate, focus-aware firewall, CSP profile, mitigation descriptions. Pure. | none |
| `packages/messaging` | `@kernl/messaging` | Messaging provider contract, registry, composite NAP-DM adapter, provider descriptions. Pure. | none |
| `packages/bridges` | `@kernl/bridges` | Locator parsing, bridge contract, registry, resource resolver with SSRF policy. Pure. | none |
| `packages/core` | `@kernl/core` | Composition root: applesauce adapters, applet resolution and mount plan, consent summaries, layouts, persistence. Browser-agnostic. | none |
| `apps/web` | `@kernl/web` | Landing site at `/` and the shell at `/app/`. | Astro 7, Svelte 5 islands |
| `docs` | `@kernl/docs` | Documentation at `/docs/`. | VitePress |

Published packages have zero framework dependencies, matching kehto's rule. The app is free to use Svelte.

**Consequences.** TypeDoc runs over the four packages. Each has a `docs/packages/<name>.md` page with a version row, enforced by `scripts/audit-docs.mjs`.

**Reversal cost.** Medium. Merging packages is cheap; splitting the app later is not.

## D-005 · Behaviour is specified in Gherkin and executed by vitest

**Context.** The requirement is BDD with full coverage. kehto and napplet both use plain vitest.

**Decision.** Every package has a `features/` directory of `.feature` files run by [quickpickle](https://github.com/dnotes/quickpickle) inside vitest, with step definitions in `features/steps/`. Coverage thresholds are 100% for statements, branches, functions and lines over `packages/*/src`. Plain `*.test.ts` files are allowed only for property-style checks that do not read as behaviour; they do not substitute for a feature.

**Consequences.** A behaviour without a scenario is not merged. Coverage is enforced in CI through `vitest run --coverage`.

**Reversal cost.** Low mechanically, high culturally.

## D-006 · The public site never names a protocol

**Context.** Requirement five: the website is gorgeous and does not say the protocol's name.

**Decision.** `apps/web` output is scanned by `scripts/check-public-vocabulary.mjs` for a denylist (`nostr`, `nip-`, `napplet`, `relay`, `pubkey`, `npub`, `nsec`) and the build fails on a hit. The denylist applies to the landing pages and the shell UI copy. It does not apply to `docs/`, which is written for developers and must name things precisely.

**Consequences.** UI copy says "applet", "account", "network", "provider", "guard". Developer-facing terms live in the docs.

**Reversal cost.** Low.

## D-007 · The site is agent-readable by construction

**Context.** Requirement: an agent-readiness score of 84 or higher, `llms.txt`, WebMCP where sensible.

**Decision.** The Astro build emits `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, a Markdown twin for every page with `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`, `/robots.txt` that allows the common AI crawlers and references the sitemap, JSON-LD (`WebApplication`, `SoftwareSourceCode`), Open Graph and canonical metadata, and semantic forms with WebMCP declarative attributes plus a guarded `navigator.modelContext.registerTool` registration. The docs build emits `/docs/llms.txt` and `/docs/llms-full.txt`. `scripts/audit-agent-readiness.mjs` checks the built artifact for every item.

**Consequences.** Agent discovery is part of the build contract, not a later task.

**Reversal cost.** Low.

## D-008 · Repository and deployment

**Context.** The GitHub organisation is `kernlize`; the repository is `kernlize/web`. No custom domain is decided.

**Decision.** URLs in package metadata point at `https://github.com/kernlize/web`. The Pages artifact is built with a configurable `SITE_BASE` (default `/`) and `SITE_URL`; the Pages workflow reads both from repository variables and falls back to `/web/` and `https://kernlize.github.io/web/`. When a domain is chosen, only the variables change. See D-013 for why production should be a domain root.

**Consequences.** Absolute URLs in `llms.txt`, sitemap, canonical tags and JSON-LD are derived from `SITE_URL` at build time.

**Reversal cost.** Low.

## D-009 · Messaging providers describe themselves; the shell does not rank them

**Context.** Opinion five.

**Decision.** `MessagingProvider.properties` is a fixed, truthful set of fields (forward secrecy, post-compromise security, metadata protection, same-client requirement, group support, specification reference). The shell renders these fields verbatim in the provider picker. There is no "recommended" flag. The first draft ships three providers: `private` (gift-wrapped private messages), `legacy` (the original direct-message format, marked as metadata-exposing), and `ratchet` (double-ratchet sessions, marked experimental and available only when its runtime is supplied).

**Consequences.** Adding a provider is a package change plus a docs page. Removing the ranking is not possible because there is none.

**Reversal cost.** Low.

## D-010 · Bridges are named by what they do

**Context.** Opinion four.

**Decision.** `@kernl/bridges` defines a `Bridge` with a user-facing `label` (`downloads`, `mail`) and a list of locator schemes (`magnet:`, `nzb:`, `slsk:`, `mailto:`). The first draft ships a complete HTTP bridge with SSRF policy and four parsers with backend interfaces (`TorrentBackend`, `NzbBackend`, `SoulseekBackend`, `MailBackend`). Without a backend, a bridge reports `unavailable` and the shell shows that honestly. Backends are out of scope for this draft and are tracked in `docs/roadmap.md`.

**Consequences.** The bridge contract is exercised end to end by the HTTP bridge, so later backends plug into a tested path.

**Reversal cost.** Low.

## D-011 · Preview mode is a product feature, not a test double

**Context.** The shell needs to be usable without an account, a network or a published applet: for people evaluating it, for the Playwright suite, and for the landing page's "open" form when nothing real is reachable.

**Decision.** `apps/web/src/shell/preview-kernl.ts` implements the same `Kernl` contract as `@kernl/core` using the real `@kernl/guard`, `@kernl/messaging` (memory backend with a scripted correspondent) and `@kernl/bridges` packages, a real applesauce `AccountManager`, and two sample applets whose `srcdoc` carries the guard's CSP and exercises consent, notifications, flooding and link opening. `?preview=1` selects it; the live path falls back to it only when `createKernl` is unavailable, and says so in a notice.

**Consequences.** Preview behaviour is held to the same vocabulary and accessibility rules as the live shell. Sample applets are the first place a new mitigation is demonstrated.

**Reversal cost.** Low; the preview is one module behind the contract.

## D-012 · Guard enforcement is layered: configured before dispatch, reactive after

**Context.** kehto's bridge owns the `MessagePort` an applet speaks over, and exposes applet traffic to the host only through the observe-only `onNappletMessage` hook. kernl cannot sit between the port and the runtime (D-001).

**Decision.** Two layers. Before dispatch, kernl configures kehto's own runtime firewall from the guard profile when an applet is mounted (`applyRuntimeFirewallRules`, translating op classes through `RUNTIME_OP_CLASSES`), so kehto rejects over-budget envelopes itself. After dispatch, kernl's ingress guard, visibility gate and focus firewall observe the same traffic with the shell's focus and visibility; a `quarantine` disposition revokes the applet's binding, and every other non-pass disposition is surfaced to the user as a guard event. The window-level `hello` is the one message kernl filters before kehto sees it.

**Consequences.** Deferral while hidden is advisory in this draft: the applet's envelope has already reached the runtime by the time the gate observes it, so the gate's effect is the tightened budget and the event trail, not a held queue. The upstream request that would make it a true pre-dispatch hook is recorded with D-001's gaps.

**Reversal cost.** Low; the pipeline sits behind `createGuardPipeline` and shrinks when kehto exposes a pre-dispatch hook.

## D-013 · The site is served at a domain root

**Context.** D-007 sets an agent-readiness score of 84 or higher. Measured with amiagentready on 2026-11-03, the scanner works on the **origin**: it scores the domain's homepage whatever path it is given, and reads `robots.txt` and `llms.txt` from the domain root. The scoring is reproducible from its response: each scored check contributes its weight, pass at full, warn at half, fail at zero.

**Measurement.** The Pages artifact served at the root of a temporary public origin, through `scripts/serve-pages.mjs`, scored **92** (12 pass, 2 warn, 0 fail; WebMCP detected). The two warns are "online booking" (kernl has none) and "schema coverage" (asks for local-business types such as opening hours and ratings, which do not apply). The same origin hosts `/docs/`, so the one score covers the website and the docs.

**Decision.** Production serves the Pages artifact at the root of its own domain, and the host answers `Accept: text/markdown` with the page's Markdown twin (`Vary: Accept`), as `scripts/serve-pages.mjs` does. The Pages workflow reads `SITE_URL` and `SITE_BASE` from repository variables, so a custom domain needs no code change.

**Consequences.** Served from the project subpath `kernlize.github.io/web/` (D-008's default), the score drops to about 82 because the origin has no `robots.txt` or `llms.txt`. A static host without content negotiation scores 90 at a root. Both regressions are visible in `docs/how-tos/deploy.md`.

**Production, 2026-11-03.** The artifact is published to the public `kernlize/kernlize.github.io` repository (built output only; this repository stays private) and served at https://kernlize.github.io/. Live amiagentready score: **90**, no failing checks; the site and `/docs/` share the score because the tool grades the origin. The browser suite, including the public-vocabulary walk-through, passes against the live URL (`PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=https://kernlize.github.io`).

**Publishing is manual, by the maintainer's choice (2026-11-03).** `pnpm site:publish` builds, runs the vocabulary and agent-readiness gates, and pushes `.pages/` to the site repository. CI builds and audits on every push; it would publish only if a scoped `SITE_PUBLISH_TOKEN` were added, and none is.

**Reversal cost.** Low; only deployment configuration.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

The failures people actually hit with this draft, what each one looks like, and what fixes it. Reason strings are listed in [Error reasons](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/reference/errors.md).

## `pnpm site:dev` before `pnpm build`

**Symptom.** The dev server starts, but the shell at `/app/` fails to load: Vite reports that it cannot resolve an `@kernl/…` import, or the shell opens the preview with the notice "Running the preview: The live shell could not start (…)".

**Cause.** `apps/web` depends on the four packages with `workspace:^`, and each package's `exports` point at `dist/index.js`. A fresh clone has no `dist/`; `pnpm install` links the packages but does not build them.

**Fix.** Build once, then start the site. Rebuild after changing a package.

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm site:dev
```

## TypeDoc fails on the git remote

**Symptom.** `pnpm docs:api` (and therefore `pnpm docs:check` and `pnpm site:build`) stops with `The provided git remote "origin" was not valid. Source links will be broken`, raised to an error by `treatWarningsAsErrors` in `typedoc.json`.

**Cause.** When neither `disableSources` nor `sourceLinkTemplate` is configured, TypeDoc derives source links from the remote named `origin` and warns when it is missing.

**Fix.** The repository's `typedoc.json` sets `packageOptions.disableSources`, which makes TypeDoc skip the remote lookup; if you see the warning, check that a local change did not remove it. `entryPointStrategy` is `packages`, so command-line flags such as `--disableSources` do not reach the per-package converters; set options under `packageOptions`. Alternatively add the remote with `git remote add origin <url>`.

## `localStorage` warnings under Node 25 and later

**Symptom.** Running `pnpm test` prints `ExperimentalWarning: localStorage is not available because --localstorage-file was not provided.`, or a test that uses `localStorage` throws because it is `undefined`.

**Cause.** Newer Node versions define a global `localStorage` that is empty unless Node is started with `--localstorage-file`. On Node 26, reading it prints the warning and returns `undefined`. kehto's shell persists its ACL and manifest cache through `localStorage`.

**Fix.** Nothing, for the shipped suites: `packages/core/features/steps/world.ts` installs an in-memory `localStorage` when the global has no `getItem`, and the warning is harmless. In your own tests, pass a `StorageLike` (a `Map` behind `getItem`, `setItem` and `removeItem`) as `KernlHost.storage`, and install a stand-in before importing kehto if your test reaches its persistence.

## An applet opens but never gets past its first screen

**Symptom.** The window shows the applet, which waits forever, shows its own "not available" state, or gets refusals.

**Cause.** A domain the applet `requires` is not granted. kernl never grants a domain because an applet asked for it: the launcher shows the required domains as switches that start off, warns "Without …, this applet may not work. You can still run it.", and `plan.missingRequired` names what is missing. The applet's `shell.init` lists only the baseline and the domains you turned on.

**Fix.** Open the window's **Grants** panel and turn the domain on. The grant reaches the ACL at once, but the domains the applet was told about at mount do not change until it is opened again, so close the window and open the applet again. If the launcher instead says "Could not open the applet (invalid:domain).", you switched on a domain this shell does not offer; turn that switch off and click **Run** again. A domain the shell does not offer has no switch in the grants panel (for example `config`, `intent` or `upload`; see [Architecture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md#where-each-nap-domain-is-served-from)), and the applet cannot get it in kernl. A new build of an applet has a new hash, so it starts with no grants; see [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md).

## An applet was quarantined

**Symptom.** A notice says "… was stopped", the window shows "This applet was stopped." with the reason `quarantine`, and the guard panel (*Guard · strict · N*) lists "Applet … was quarantined: it kept flooding the shell" (`flood:quarantine`) or "…: too many web fetches while hidden" (`flood:hidden-resource`).

**Cause.** The applet sent more messages than the profile allows in the rolling window, or used up its `resource.*` allowance while hidden. The guard revokes the applet's binding and removes its frame; the guard state for that window is dropped.

**Fix.** A stopped window does not restart. The window's **Grants** panel offers **Release from quarantine**, which calls `kernl.guard.release(windowId)` and clears the window's quarantine mark; to run the applet again, close the stopped window and open the applet again. It gets a fresh window and fresh guard counters, and its grants are unchanged, because quarantine does not block. If it floods again, either block it (**Block applet**) or, for an applet you trust, switch the guard panel's profile; that applies to every window and resets to `strict` on reload ([Change the guard profile](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/change-guard-profile.md)).

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/add-a-bridge-backend.md -->

# Add a bridge backend

The four non-HTTP bridges are complete up to the backend interface they call. Supplying a backend turns `unavailable` into a working bridge without touching the parser, the registry or the consent path, all of which the HTTP bridge already exercises. This how-to supplies a `TorrentBackend`; the others follow the same shape.

## 1. Pick the interface

| Bridge | Label | Interface | Method | Locator fields used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `torrent` | `downloads` | `TorrentBackend` | `add(infoHash, trackers, context) → Promise<{ id, name }>` | `infoHash`, `trackers` (may be empty) |
| `nzb` | `downloads` | `NzbBackend` | `add(url, context) → Promise<{ id, name }>` | `url` |
| `soulseek` | `sharing` | `SoulseekBackend` | `download(user, path, context) → Promise<{ id, name }>` | `user`, `path` |
| `mail` | `mail` | `MailBackend` | `open(address, subject, context) → Promise<{ id }>` | `address`, `subject` (`undefined` when absent) |

`context` is the `BridgeContext` the registry passes through: the requester identity (or `'shell'`), an optional `AbortSignal` and optional headers. Honour the signal when it is present. The bridge reads the fields before calling you and rejects with `invalid:locator-missing-<field>` if one is missing, so inside the backend they are guaranteed strings; `trackers` is always a list.

## 2. Implement it outside the published packages

A backend talks to something: a WebTorrent client, a downloader daemon, a mail account. That belongs in the host app (`apps/web`, or your own page) or in a package of its own with its own dependencies, not in `@kernl/bridges`, which stays dependency-free. The samples on this page type-check against the built packages.

```ts
import type { BridgeContext, TorrentBackend } from '@kernl/bridges';

interface WebTorrentLike {
  add(magnet: string): { infoHash: string; name: string; ready: Promise<void> };
  remove(torrent: { infoHash: string }): void;
}

export function createWebTorrentBackend(client: WebTorrentLike): TorrentBackend {
  return {
    async add(infoHash, trackers, context: BridgeContext) {
      const magnet = `magnet:?xt=urn:btih:${infoHash}${trackers.map((t) => `&tr=${encodeURIComponent(t)}`).join('')}`;
      const torrent = client.add(magnet);
      context.signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => client.remove(torrent), { once: true });
      await torrent.ready;
      return { id: torrent.infoHash, name: torrent.name };
    },
  };
}
```

Return a stable `id`: it is the job's identity in the `202` body the applet receives, and what a future downloads view would use to show state and cancel. The `name` becomes the job's `label`. Reject with stable reasons (`unavailable:engine-offline`, `denied:…`); the registry reports and rethrows them unchanged (`registry.feature`, scenario "a bridge failure is reported and rethrown").

## 3. Hand it to the bridge

`createTorrentBridge(backend?)` takes the backend as an optional argument. Without one it reports `{ available: false, reason: 'no-backend' }` and rejects every `resolve()` with `unavailable:no-backend`; with one it reports available and routes `resolve()` to `backend.add`.

The shell's bridges are registered by `createDefaultBridges` in `packages/core/src/bridges/default-registry.ts`, which `createKernl` calls when `KernlOptions.bridges` is absent. Its signature is `createDefaultBridges(options?: DefaultBridgesOptions)`, where the options are the registry's `authorize` and `onResolve` plus `http` for the web bridge. It takes no backends, and a registry cannot replace a bridge it already holds (a second `torrent` throws `invalid:duplicate-bridge torrent`). So a host that supplies a backend builds the same five registrations itself, with its backend in place, and passes the registry as `KernlOptions.bridges`:

```ts
import { createKernl, type KernlHost } from '@kernl/core';
import {
  createBridgeRegistry,
  createHttpBridge,
  createMailBridge,
  createNzbBridge,
  createSoulseekBridge,
  createTorrentBridge,
  type BridgeRegistry,
  type TorrentBackend,
} from '@kernl/bridges';

declare const host: KernlHost;
declare const client: Parameters<typeof createWebTorrentBackend>[0];

export function createBridgesWithTorrent(torrent: TorrentBackend): BridgeRegistry {
  const registry = createBridgeRegistry({ onResolve: (event) => console.info('bridge', event) });
  registry.register(createHttpBridge());
  registry.register(createTorrentBridge(torrent));
  registry.register(createNzbBridge());
  registry.register(createSoulseekBridge());
  registry.register(createMailBridge());
  return registry;
}

const kernl = createKernl({ host, bridges: createBridgesWithTorrent(createWebTorrentBackend(client)) });
kernl.bridges.forScheme('magnet')?.availability(); // { available: true }
```

The web, NZB, Soulseek and mail bridges are the same as the defaults. To ship the backend inside kernl itself, change the torrent registration in `createDefaultBridges` instead.

Check the bridge's `exposure`. The torrent bridge declares `revealsAddress: true`, `encryptedInTransit: false`, `publicActivity: true`, which is the truth for a client in a public swarm. The factory does not take an exposure argument, so if your backend changes the truth of any field (a backend that tunnels through a seedbox does not reveal the user's address), register a bridge object with the same `resolve` and a corrected `exposure`:

```ts
const stock = createTorrentBridge(createWebTorrentBackend(client));
registry.register({ ...stock, exposure: { ...stock.exposure, revealsAddress: false } });
```

Register that object in place of `createTorrentBridge(torrent)` in `createBridgesWithTorrent`.

The user reads these three booleans, rendered by `describeBridge`, before consenting; they must be right.

## 4. What already applies, and what does not yet

`BridgeRegistry.resolve` checks `availability()`, then calls the registry's `authorize` hook if one was given, before any bridge runs; a denial rejects with `denied:bridge`. The composed shell wires no `BridgeAuthorizer`: `createKernl` uses `createDefaultBridges()` without `authorize`, so a request from an applet that holds the `resource` grant reaches your bridge without a per-request prompt. A host that wants one passes `authorize` to `createBridgeRegistry` in the sample above; a consent prompt per host in the shell is on the [Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md#_6-guard) ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#what-does-not-work-yet)).

The guard's `resource:bytes` rate and hidden-window allowance apply to `resource.*` envelopes. A `job` result reaches kehto's resource service as a `202 Accepted` JSON body through `createBridgeResourceResolver`; the applet that asked receives it. The shell has no downloads list yet, so nothing shows job state to the user; that UI is roadmap work. Every outcome is also reported to `onResolve` as a `BridgeResolveEvent`.

## 5. Specify and document

- `packages/bridges/features/backend-bridges.feature` already covers the contract with a fake backend: unavailable without a backend, fields handed through, missing fields rejected. Add scenarios for what your backend adds: an aborted context cancels the job; the engine's failure reasons surface unchanged.
- Move the backend's row from "unavailable" to "available" in [Bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md#backend-driven-bridges) and strike it from the [Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md).
- Add a changeset.

The slop gate and the coverage threshold apply to the backend if it lives in `packages/`. If it lives in `apps/web`, the Playwright suite in `pnpm test:e2e` covers it.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/add-a-messaging-provider.md -->

# Add a messaging provider

A provider is a package change plus a docs page. This how-to adds a provider called `example` and wires it into the shell's registry.

## 1. Describe it truthfully

Start with the properties, because they are the contract with the user. Every field except `specification` is required, and the shell shows all of them except `specification` through `describeProvider`.

```ts
import type { ProviderDefinition, SecurityProperties } from '@kernl/messaging';

export const EXAMPLE_PROPERTIES: SecurityProperties = {
  forwardSecrecy: false,
  postCompromiseSecurity: false,
  metadataProtection: 'partial',
  requiresSameClient: true,
  groups: false,
  specification: 'https://example.org/spec',
  experimental: true,
};

export const EXAMPLE_DEFINITION: ProviderDefinition = {
  id: 'example',
  name: 'Example messages',
  description: 'Messages readable by other people using this shell.',
  properties: EXAMPLE_PROPERTIES,
};
```

If you are unsure whether a property holds, it does not. A provider that overstates its protection fails the review, however good its code is. `name` and `description` are shown in the public UI, so they follow the [public vocabulary](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/public-vocabulary.md): no protocol names. `specification` is where the protocol name goes; `describeProvider` never renders it.

## 2. Implement the backend

A `MessagingBackend` has six methods and an optional `close`. Ids you return are provider-local; the composite prefixes them with `example:`. Wire types come from `@napplet/core`. The backend talks to whatever the shell hands it; here that is a small `ExampleDeps` object so the sample stays free of any relay library.

```ts
import type { DmMessage, DmSendRequest, DmSendResult } from '@napplet/core';
import type { MessagingBackend } from '@kernl/messaging';

export interface ExampleDeps {
  readonly ownerPubkey: string;
  readonly publish: (request: DmSendRequest) => Promise<DmMessage>;
  readonly history: (conversationId: string) => readonly DmMessage[];
  readonly onIncoming: (listener: (message: DmMessage) => void) => () => void;
}

export function createExampleBackend(deps: ExampleDeps): MessagingBackend {
  const subscriptions = new Map<string, () => void>();
  let count = 0;
  return {
    status: () => ({ available: true, ownerPubkey: deps.ownerPubkey, implementations: ['example'], capabilities: ['send', 'receive', 'subscribe', 'history'] }),
    conversations: () => ({ conversations: [] }),
    messages: (query) => ({ messages: [...deps.history(query.conversationId)] }),
    async send(request): Promise<DmSendResult> {
      if (request.recipients.length === 0) throw new Error('invalid:no-recipients');
      return { ok: true, message: await deps.publish(request) };
    },
    subscribe(request, onMessage) {
      count += 1;
      const subscriptionId = `example-${count}`;
      subscriptions.set(
        subscriptionId,
        deps.onIncoming((message) => {
          if (request.conversationId === undefined || message.conversationId === request.conversationId) onMessage(message);
        }),
      );
      return { subscriptionId };
    },
    unsubscribe(subscriptionId) {
      const stop = subscriptions.get(subscriptionId);
      stop?.();
      return { ok: subscriptions.delete(subscriptionId) };
    },
    close() {
      for (const stop of subscriptions.values()) stop();
      subscriptions.clear();
    },
  };
}
```

Rules the backend must keep:

- Use the shell's shared `EventStore` and `RelayPool` (`kernl.eventStore`, `kernl.pool`); do not open a second relay connection. The shell does not inject anything into your backend: `@kernl/core` calls only the factory you register, so you build `ExampleDeps` yourself from those instances, as `exampleDeps(resolve)` below does.
- Sign only through the function the shell injects. Never touch key bytes.
- Reject with stable reasons: `denied:`, `invalid:`, `unavailable:`.
- `subscribe` returns `{ subscriptionId }`; `unsubscribe` of an unknown id returns `{ ok: false }`; `close` drops every subscription. Every method except `send` may be synchronous.
- Page with `cursor` and `limit`. The composite passes your cursor through when you are the only enabled provider, so make it a string you can resume from.

Use `createMemoryBackend` as the reference for the semantics the features expect, and as the backend in your own tests.

## 3. Build the provider with `defineProvider`

The registry calls `createBackend()` once per enable and `available()` whenever it needs to know. Both are injected, so this package never learns what a session is:

```ts
import { defineProvider, type ProviderDeps } from '@kernl/messaging';

export function exampleDeps(resolve: () => ExampleDeps | undefined): ProviderDeps {
  return {
    createBackend: () => {
      const deps = resolve();
      if (!deps) throw new Error('unavailable:signed-out');
      return createExampleBackend(deps);
    },
    available: () => (resolve() ? { available: true } : { available: false, reason: 'signed-out' }),
  };
}

const provider = defineProvider(EXAMPLE_DEFINITION, exampleDeps(() => currentSessionDeps()));
```

The `reason` is a bare word. The registry prefixes it: `enable('example')` throws `unavailable:signed-out`, and `list()` reports `{ available: false, reason: 'signed-out' }` so the picker can grey the provider and say why.

The three built-ins (`createPrivateMessagesProvider`, `createLegacyMessagesProvider`, `createRatchetMessagesProvider`) are exactly this shape: a fixed definition in the package, `ProviderDeps` from the shell. If your provider ships in `@kernl/messaging`, add `createExampleMessagesProvider(deps: ProviderDeps)` next to them in `packages/messaging/src/providers/` and export it from `providers/index.ts`.

## 4. Register it

The three built-in providers are registered by `createDefaultMessaging` in `packages/core/src/messaging/default-registry.ts`, which `createKernl` calls when `KernlOptions.messaging` is absent. You do not edit `createKernl`. A host has two options-based paths:

- **A backend for a built-in provider.** Pass `KernlOptions.messagingBackends`, a `MessagingBackendFactories` (`{ private?, legacy?, ratchet? }`, each `() => MessagingBackend`). The provider whose factory you supply reports itself available.
- **A new provider.** Build the default registry yourself, register yours on it, and pass it as `KernlOptions.messaging`. The defaults stay registered:

```ts
import { createDefaultMessaging, createKernl, type KernlHost } from '@kernl/core';

declare const host: KernlHost;

const messaging = createDefaultMessaging({ storage: host.storage });
messaging.register(provider);
const kernl = createKernl({ host, messaging });
```

When `messaging` is supplied, `createKernl` uses it as is and ignores `messagingBackends`; pass any built-in backends to `createDefaultMessaging({ storage, backends })` instead. To ship a provider inside kernl itself, register it in `createDefaultMessaging` next to the three built-ins.

Registration does not enable, unless the user's saved preferences already list `example`; then it is enabled on registration if `available()` agrees, and left disabled otherwise. The user enables it in the provider picker, which calls `registry.enable('example')`. Registering the same id twice throws `invalid:duplicate-provider`. See `registry.feature`, scenarios "a registered provider starts disabled" and "saved preferences enable providers as they register".

## 5. Specify and document

- Add the provider to the `Scenario Outline` in `packages/messaging/features/providers.feature` ("the built-in providers carry fixed copy and properties") with its name, description, six properties and specification, and a scenario that `describeProvider` rows name no protocol. Step definitions live in `packages/messaging/features/steps/`.
- If the backend lives in a package, give it a feature file modelled on `memory-backend.feature`: sends create conversations, delivered messages are unread, subscriptions filter by conversation, cursors resume.
- Add a row to the providers table in [Messaging](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md#the-three-providers) and a line to the providers table on the [package page](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/messaging.md#providers).
- Add a changeset for `@kernl/messaging` (and `@kernl/core` if you touched `createDefaultMessaging`).

`pnpm test` must stay at 100% coverage over `packages/*/src`, and `pnpm docs:check` must pass. A provider without the feature rows or the docs rows is not shipped.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/change-guard-profile.md -->

# Change the guard profile

The shell boots every applet in `strict`. A user can loosen one applet to `balanced` or `relaxed`. There is no way to loosen every applet at once, and that is the point ([D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003)).

## In the shell

1. Open the guard panel from the desktop bar (*Guard · strict · N*).
2. Under *Profile*, pick `balanced` or `relaxed`. The list of mitigations updates to show the new limit for each one. The CSP does not change; it never does.
3. The change calls `kernl.guard.setProfile(profile)`, which rebuilds every guard layer for every open window at once; held messages are dropped and counters restart, so a quarantined window is released. It is not persisted: a reload starts in `strict` again.

In this draft the profile is shell-wide. The per-applet, remembered override that [D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003) describes is listed under [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#what-does-not-work-yet).

## In code

A profile is a `GuardConfig` from `createGuardConfig(profile)`. The three guard layers each take that config in an options object, together with an optional clock and an event sink:

```ts
import {
  createFocusFirewall,
  createGuardConfig,
  createIngressGuard,
  createVisibilityGate,
  type GuardEvent,
  type GuardProfile,
} from '@kernl/guard';

function guardFor(profile: GuardProfile, onEvent: (event: GuardEvent) => void) {
  const config = createGuardConfig(profile);
  return {
    config,
    ingress: createIngressGuard({ config, onEvent }),
    gate: createVisibilityGate({ config, onEvent }),
    firewall: createFocusFirewall({ config, onEvent }),
  };
}
```

`now` defaults to `Date.now` in all three; inject it in tests. Switching a mounted window from one profile to another means, at the guard level:

1. Build the three layers from the new config. The layers hold no reference to the profile, so there is no in-place update; the old `IngressGuard`, `VisibilityGate` and `FocusFirewall` are replaced.
2. Drain what the old gate and old ingress guard still hold (`drain(windowId)`) and admit it through the new layers, so nothing queued is lost.
3. Call `release(windowId)` on the old ingress guard, or simply drop it: quarantine lives in the guard instance and does not survive the swap.
4. If the shell also runs kehto's runtime firewall from `config.firewall`, hand it the new `FirewallConfig`. Per-applet rates are not in a fresh config; `applyNappletRules(config, dTag)` adds them, and the focus firewall does this itself on first observation.

`@kernl/core` does this inside `createGuardPipeline`: `GuardFacade.setProfile(profile)` rebuilds the three layers from `createGuardConfig(profile)`, clears what they held, re-applies the known visibility of every window and emits on `profile$`; `GuardFacade.release(windowId)` lifts a quarantine on its own. Applets mounted after the change get the new profile's rates in kehto's runtime firewall through `applyRuntimeFirewallRules`; windows already open keep the runtime rates they were mounted with until they are opened again. The [core page](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md#the-kernl-surface) documents that surface.

## What a profile cannot change

- The Content Security Policy. `createAppletCsp(profile)` returns the same policy for every profile; see [why](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#why-csp-never-loosens) and `csp.feature`, scenario "the relaxed profile does not loosen the CSP".
- Whether a mitigation is enabled. Every profile enables all eleven; `describeMitigations(config)` only changes the `limit` text.
- Grants. A profile is about rate, not authority. [Grant and revoke](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/grant-and-revoke.md) covers authority.

## What a profile changes

Exact values for every limit and every per-class rate are in [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#profiles). In one line each: `balanced` raises the headline limits by 1.5× to 2× (`ingressBurst` 8 → 12, `ingressQueue` 64 → 128, `quarantineThreshold` 300 → 420, `hiddenResourceAllowance` 8 → 16, `deferQueue` 200 → 400, envelope caps 64/256 KiB → 128/512 KiB, `unfocusedMultiplier` 0.25 → 0.5) and doubles every rate; `relaxed` goes to 24, 192, 800, 32, 600, 192/768 KiB and 0.75, and triples every rate.

## Adding a profile

Do not. Three is the number the UI was designed around, and a fourth profile would be a developer deciding how much an applet may do, which `SOUL.md` reserves for the user. If an applet needs a limit no profile provides, that is a reason to revisit the limits in `strict`, with a scenario in `packages/guard/features/profiles.feature` that shows the applet a competent developer could not otherwise build.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/deploy.md -->

# Deploy

kernl deploys as one static artifact: the landing site at the root, the shell at `/app/`, the docs at `/docs/` and the generated API reference at `/docs/api/`. `scripts/build-pages.mjs` assembles it into `.pages/`, and GitHub Pages serves it. No server-side code is involved.

## The three variables

| Variable | Used by | Meaning | Default | Pages value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SITE_URL` | Astro site, docs `llms.txt` | Absolute URL of the deployment root. Canonical tags, sitemap, JSON-LD and the absolute links in `llms.txt` are derived from it. | `https://kernlize.github.io/` | `https://kernlize.github.io/` |
| `SITE_BASE` | Astro site | Path prefix the site is served under. | `/` | `/` |
| `VITEPRESS_BASE` | Docs site | Path prefix the docs are served under. Always `SITE_BASE` plus `docs/`. | `/docs/` | `/docs/` |

The Pages workflow reads `SITE_URL` and `SITE_BASE` from repository variables (`vars.SITE_URL`, `vars.SITE_BASE`) and falls back to the domain root: `https://kernlize.github.io/` and `/`. It sets `VITEPRESS_BASE` to `SITE_BASE` followed by `docs/`. When a custom domain is chosen, set those two variables; nothing in the source references a host ([D-008](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-008)).

## Serve at a domain root

The site is served at the root of its own origin, **https://kernlize.github.io/**, because agent-readiness scanners grade the origin: they read `robots.txt` and `llms.txt` from the domain root whatever path they are given, and a project subpath such as `kernlize.github.io/web/` has neither ([D-013](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-013)).

The source repository is private, so it does not serve Pages itself. The built `.pages/` artifact is published to the public `kernlize/kernlize.github.io` repository, which holds nothing else. Publishing is manual by decision ([D-013](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-013)): one command builds, runs the vocabulary and agent-readiness gates, and pushes the artifact.

```bash
pnpm site:publish
```

`.github/workflows/pages.yml` builds and audits the same artifact on every push to `main`. It publishes only if a `SITE_PUBLISH_TOKEN` secret (a fine-grained token with Contents read/write on `kernlize/kernlize.github.io`) is ever added; none is configured.

To move to a custom domain, set the `SITE_URL` repository variable to `https://<domain>/`, keep `SITE_BASE` at `/`, and add a `CNAME` file to the published artifact. GitHub Pages cannot answer `Accept: text/markdown`; a host that should needs a rule that serves the page's `.md` twin with `Vary: Accept`. `scripts/serve-pages.mjs` implements the rule and is the reference.

## Build locally

```bash
pnpm site:build
```

This runs, in order: `pnpm build` (packages), `pnpm docs:check` (TypeDoc, VitePress, the docs audit), the Astro build, then `node scripts/build-pages.mjs`. The result is `.pages/`:

```
.pages/
├── index.html            landing site
├── app/                  shell
├── llms.txt              site index (Astro)
├── docs/
│   ├── index.html        VitePress
│   ├── llms.txt          docs index
│   ├── llms-full.txt
│   ├── **/*.md           Markdown twins
│   └── api/              TypeDoc
└── .nojekyll
```

`build-pages.mjs` fails if any input is missing, so a half-built artifact is never produced. `PAGES_OUT_DIR` overrides the output directory.

## Preview the artifact

```bash
pnpm site:preview
```

`scripts/serve-pages.mjs` serves `.pages/` on `http://127.0.0.1:4178/`. To preview under the Pages prefix exactly as deployed:

```bash
SITE_BASE=/web/ VITEPRESS_BASE=/web/docs/ pnpm site:build
PAGES_PREVIEW_PATH=/web/ pnpm site:preview
# → http://127.0.0.1:4178/web/
```

The server resolves directory URLs to `index.html` and VitePress clean URLs to their `.html` file, answers `Accept: text/markdown` with the page's Markdown twin (`Vary: Accept`), serves `.md` as `text/markdown` and `.txt` as `text/plain`, and refuses paths outside the artifact.

## Publish workflow

`.github/workflows/pages.yml` runs on pushes to `main`:

```yaml
env:
  SITE_URL: ${{ vars.SITE_URL || 'https://kernlize.github.io/' }}
  SITE_BASE: ${{ vars.SITE_BASE || '/' }}
  VITEPRESS_BASE: ${{ vars.SITE_BASE || '/' }}docs/
steps:
  - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
  - run: pnpm site:build
  - run: pnpm check:vocabulary
  - run: pnpm check:agent-ready
  - name: Publish to kernlize/kernlize.github.io   # needs SITE_PUBLISH_TOKEN
```

`pnpm site:build` includes the docs gate, so a deployment with a missing package page, a missing Markdown twin or a broken TypeDoc module does not happen. `pnpm check:vocabulary` and `pnpm check:agent-ready` run in the same workflow against `.pages/`.

## TypeDoc source links

`typedoc.json` sets `packageOptions.disableSources`, so the generated reference carries no links into the source repository, which is private during the alpha, and TypeDoc never consults a git remote. Because `entryPointStrategy` is `packages`, command-line flags such as `--disableSources` do not reach the per-package converters; set source options under `packageOptions`. When the repository opens, replace it with a `sourceLinkTemplate` pointing at the public tree. Without either option, TypeDoc looks up the `origin` remote and, if there is none, warns; `treatWarningsAsErrors` turns that into a failed `pnpm docs:api` ([Troubleshooting](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md#typedoc-fails-on-the-git-remote)).

## Hosting somewhere else

Any static host works. Set `SITE_URL` to the deployment root, `SITE_BASE` and `VITEPRESS_BASE` to its path prefix (usually `/` and `/docs/`), build, and upload `.pages/`. The shell has no server dependency; the applets it opens come from relays the user chose.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/embed-kernl-core.md -->

# Embed kernl core

`apps/web` is one host for `@kernl/core`; your own page can be another. This how-to implements `KernlHost`, calls `createKernl`, and mounts an applet in an iframe you own. The sample type-checks against the built packages with `strict` on.

The packages are not yet published to npm, so your page lives in a clone of the kernl source as a workspace package that depends on `@kernl/core` and `@kernl/guard` with `workspace:^`, and you run `pnpm build` first ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)).

## 1. Put the frame policy in the page head

The host page must stop applet frames from navigating away from their verified `srcdoc`. `KERNL_FRAME_POLICY_META` is the `<meta>` element that does it, rendered once by kehto's `renderNappletFramePolicyMeta`:

```html
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-src 'none'">
```

Put it in the `<head>` of the HTML the server sends, before any script runs, as `apps/web/src/pages/app/index.astro` does. If your page is generated, render the constant into the head at build time (`import { KERNL_FRAME_POLICY_META } from '@kernl/core'`) rather than inserting it from client code, so the policy is in force before the first frame exists. Applets still load, because their bytes arrive as `srcdoc` rather than from a URL; a frame that tries to load or navigate to a URL is blocked.

## 2. Implement `KernlHost` and create the shell

`KernlHost` is the only way the core reaches the user or the page. Six members are required:

| Member | What the core expects |
| --- | --- |
| `storage` | A synchronous `StorageLike` (`getItem`, `setItem`, `removeItem`). `localStorage` satisfies it. Grants, accounts, relay tiers and messaging preferences persist here under `kernl:` keys. |
| `presentConsent(prompt)` | Show `prompt.summary` (title, severity, lines) and call `prompt.resolve(true \| false)`. Resolve `false` on dismiss; the core never times out. |
| `notify(notice)` | Show `{ title, body?, windowId?, tone }`. Applets reach it through the `notify` domain; the guard and revocations use it too. |
| `openLink(url)` | Open a URL outside the shell. It is called only after the link service allowed the protocol (`https:`, `mailto:`); confirming with the user is your choice. |
| `getVisibility(windowId)` | Return `{ visible, focused, msSinceFocusGain? }` for a window, synchronously. The guard uses it for hidden allowances and focus tightening. |
| `onRevoked(windowId, reason)` | Called after the core removed a frame because its binding was revoked (`quarantine`, `second-load`, …). Update your UI. |

`fetchBlob` and `now` are optional; without them the core fetches artifact blobs with `defaultFetchBlob` and uses `Date.now`.

```ts
import { createKernl, type AppletHandle, type ConsentPrompt, type KernlHost } from '@kernl/core';
import type { WindowVisibility } from '@kernl/guard';
import { ReadonlyAccount } from 'applesauce-accounts/accounts';

const frames = new Map<string, HTMLIFrameElement>();
let focusedId: string | null = null;

function visibilityOf(windowId: string): WindowVisibility {
  const frame = frames.get(windowId);
  const visible = frame !== undefined && frame.isConnected && document.visibilityState === 'visible';
  return { visible, focused: visible && focusedId === windowId };
}

function describe(prompt: ConsentPrompt): string {
  const lines = prompt.summary.lines.map((line) => `${line.label}: ${line.before ?? '-'} -> ${line.after ?? '-'}`);
  return [prompt.summary.title, ...lines].join('\n');
}

const host: KernlHost = {
  storage: localStorage,
  presentConsent: (prompt) => prompt.resolve(window.confirm(describe(prompt))),
  notify: (notice) => console.info(`[${notice.tone}] ${notice.title}${notice.body ? `: ${notice.body}` : ''}`),
  openLink: (url) => void window.open(url, '_blank', 'noopener,noreferrer'),
  getVisibility: visibilityOf,
  onRevoked(windowId, reason) {
    frames.get(windowId)?.remove();
    frames.delete(windowId);
    console.warn(`applet ${windowId} was stopped: ${reason}`);
  },
};

const kernl = createKernl({ host });
window.addEventListener('message', (event) => kernl.handleWindowMessage(event));

function refreshVisibility(): void {
  for (const handle of kernl.applets()) handle.setVisibility(visibilityOf(handle.windowId));
}
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', refreshVisibility);

export async function signInReadOnly(pubkey: string): Promise<void> {
  const session = await kernl.login(ReadonlyAccount.fromPubkey(pubkey));
  console.info(`signed in as ${session.label}, read-only: ${session.readOnly}`);
}

export async function openApplet(address: string, container: HTMLElement): Promise<AppletHandle> {
  const summary = await kernl.resolve(kernl.decodePointer(address));
  const offered = kernl.grants.availableDomains();
  const baseline = kernl.grants.baselineDomains();
  for (const domain of summary.requires) {
    if (!offered.includes(domain) || baseline.includes(domain)) continue;
    if (window.confirm(`${summary.title} says it needs "${domain}". Allow it?`)) kernl.grants.allowDomain(summary.identity, domain);
  }
  const plan = await kernl.plan(summary);
  if (plan.missingRequired.length > 0) console.warn(`${summary.title} runs without ${plan.missingRequired.join(', ')}`);

  const frame = document.createElement('iframe');
  frame.title = summary.title;
  container.append(frame);
  frames.set(plan.windowId, frame);
  container.addEventListener('pointerdown', () => {
    focusedId = plan.windowId;
    refreshVisibility();
  });
  return kernl.mount(plan, frame);
}
```

`createKernl({ host })` creates one `EventStore`, one `RelayPool` and one `AccountManager`, the guard pipeline in `strict`, the default messaging and bridge registries, kehto's services and the shell bridge ([`@kernl/core`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md#composition)). Pass any of them in `KernlOptions` to use your own. Wire `handleWindowMessage` to `window` exactly once: it is how an applet's `hello` reaches the guard and then kehto.

## 3. The mount flow

`openApplet` above is the whole lifecycle, and the order matters:

1. **`decodePointer(address)`** turns the address into a pointer and throws `invalid:pointer` for anything else.
2. **`resolve(pointer)`** fetches the manifest from the pointer's relay hints plus the `apps` tier and verifies the signature and the artifact bytes. The `AppletSummary` it returns is what you show before running anything; `requires` and `optional` are advisory.
3. **Grants.** Ask the user, then call `grants.allowDomain(identity, domain)` for what they allowed. Skip domains outside `grants.availableDomains()`, which throw `invalid:domain`, and the baseline ones, which are always on.
4. **`plan(summary)`** writes the applet's ACL explicitly and returns the `MountPlan`: the srcdoc with the guard's CSP, the environment the applet will see, and `missingRequired`. It throws `denied:blocked` for a blocked applet.
5. **The frame.** Create the iframe and attach it to the document first: `mount` needs its `contentWindow` and throws `invalid:frame-detached` otherwise. Do not set `src`, `sandbox` or `srcdoc` yourself. Record it under `plan.windowId` so `getVisibility` can answer for it.
6. **`mount(plan, frame)`** installs the profile's runtime rates, sets `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and the controller-denying `allow` policy, registers the window, and only then assigns `srcdoc`. It returns an `AppletHandle`.

After mount, keep the guard informed: call `handle.setVisibility(...)` whenever a window is shown, hidden, focused or blurred (the sample does it on `visibilitychange` and on pointer focus). `handle.close()` revokes the binding and removes the frame; grants stay, keyed by identity. `kernl.destroy()` closes everything when the page goes away.

## 4. Check it

- Open an applet that `requires` `relay` and decline it: `plan.missingRequired` is `['relay']` and the applet's `shell.init` lacks it.
- Hide its container and call `setVisibility`: from then on the applet's resource requests count against the hidden allowance, and any overrun appears on `kernl.guard.events$`.
- Subscribe to `kernl.guard.events$` and `kernl.session$` and render them; they are the same streams `apps/web` shows in its guard panel and sign-in screen.

## Related

- [Run the shell](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/run-the-shell.md), the same flow through `apps/web`
- [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md)
- [Architecture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md#the-mount-path)
- [Error reasons](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/reference/errors.md)
